sentences.text: The premise holds in a narrow sense: the filings tie the H20 license requirement to a $4.5 billion charge for excess inventory and purchase obligations, and licensed China shipments since then have been small, so export controls plainly constrained what could be sold into China.

What the record cannot show is the claim's causal half, that revenue is lower than it would otherwise be, because a forgone sale leaves no figure; the test that could be run, a year-over-year decline in China including Hong Kong revenue, fails with a margin of +97.7 points, which runs against the claim.
Company-wide, there is no visible squeeze: revenue grew 105.9% on a year earlier and growth sped up by 20.6 percentage points over the prior quarter, almost all of it from Data Center.

For an overweight position into the next report, the step from 'China is restricted' to 'results are at risk' is therefore assumed, not backed: the restriction already sits in the base the growth is measured from, and the charge it produced was a cost and inventory event rather than a revenue line.

The claim is best read as true about a constraint and beside the point for the near-term revenue print, unless the filing's warning that controls can depress demand outside China starts to show in the numbers.

The $4.5 billion charge is a filed, quantified consequence of the license requirement, and only about $60 million of H20 revenue came through under the licenses later granted, so the China channel for that product is effectively shut.
The filing itself says export controls have reduced and may reduce demand beyond China, in Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia, which would widen the restriction past one geography.
Revenue rose in each of the last 8 quarters and the latest quarter's growth accelerated, which is hard to square with export controls restricting revenue in any way that matters to the total.

The one computed test of a China revenue decline came out against the claim, by a margin of +97.7 points, and the share-of-revenue corollary could not be computed, so the record offers no figure showing China revenue shrinking.
Receivable days rose to 59.6 from 54.1 a year before, a more pressing quality-of-growth question for the next report than China, since receivables grew +126.8% against revenue's +105.9%.
Whether the restriction ever shows as a falling revenue line rather than a one-time inventory and purchase-obligation charge; so far only the charge is on record.
Whether demand effects spread beyond China as the filing warns, which would turn a contained constraint into one that touches the Data Center growth now carrying the total.

conditions.text: Quarterly revenue falling below the $96.22B of the quarter ended 2026-07-26 would be the first sign of a squeeze that export controls could plausibly be part of.
Gross margin dropping below the 75.0% of the latest quarter could reflect a further export-related inventory or purchase-obligation charge like the H20 one.
An 8-K disclosing a new export license requirement, revocation or related charge would directly test whether controls are tightening on revenue.
